slide_text: Quick Check: You run K-Means twice on the same points but with different random starting centers. What happens? A. Always the same result K-Means finds the unique best answer B. May get different final clusters K-Means is sensitive to initialization C. The second run crashes D. The second run is always worse

fragments.text: Answer: B. Different starting centers can lead to different local optima. In practice, run K-Means several times and keep the best result.

slide_text: Quick Check: Does K-Means always converge (stop changing)? A. Yes each iteration can only decrease or maintain the total distance; it must eventually stabilize B. No it can oscillate forever C. Only if k = 2 D. Only for 2D data

fragments.text: Answer: A. K-Means provably converges. Each step either reduces the total distance or leaves it unchanged. Since there are finitely many possible assignments, it must terminate.

slide_text: This is called the elbow method : plot inertia vs. k and look for the elbow the point where adding more clusters stops helping much. [code block]

fragments.text: Quick Check: Why not just use [math] (one cluster per point)? A. It doesn t converge B. Inertia = 0 but no useful grouping every point is its own cluster C. It s too slow D. Python can t handle it
Answer: B. Clustering is about discovering structure . With [math], inertia is zero but you ve learned nothing about the data.
